The diploid WT is normalised to 2 so a haploid sum of 1 is WT and a haploid sum of
2.5 is $2.5\times$ WT.  Put the cis aFC in chromosomal order $\pi_{1}\dots\pi_{5}$,
$\Pi=\prod_{i}\pi_{i}=1/3\cdot1/2\cdot3/2\cdot2\cdot3=3/2$ and
$P_{k}=\prod_{i\le k}\pi_{i}$.

With a single crossover per homologue and four heterozygous loci and one
homozygous-mutant locus the two gametes can be taken up to telomere reversal as

$H_{L}:1\ldots h\;{\rm mut},\,h+1\ldots5\;{\rm WT}$,
$H_{R}:1\ldots h-1\;{\rm WT},\,h\ldots5\;{\rm mut}$,

$E_{L}=P_{h},\qquad E_{R}= \Pi/P_{h-1}$,

$T(h)=E_{L}+E_{R}=P_{h}+\Pi/P_{h-1}=P_{h-1}\pi_{h}+\Pi/P_{h-1}$.

A genuine single crossover on each homologue between SNP1 and SNP5 needs
both gametes to be recombinant, i.e. $1<h<5$, $h=2,3,4$, an interior
homozygous site.  Put $x=P_{h-1},a=\pi_{h}$.  $T(h)=2$ gives

$a x^{2}-2x+\Pi=0$, $\Delta=4-4a\Pi\ge0\iff a\le2/3$.

Hence $a\in\{1/3,1/2\}$.  With an interior $h$ the admissible solution is

$a=\pi_{h}=1/2$, $x=P_{h-1}=1$,

$P_{h}=1/2,\;Q_{h}=\Pi/x=3/2,\;T(h)=2$.

Up to reversal this is $h_{WT}=4$ with $P_{3}=1,\;\pi_{4}=1/2$.

Now $T(k)=5$.  With $P_{3}=1$ the interior solution is $k=2$:

$T(2)=P_{2}+\Pi/\pi_{1}=5,\qquad P_{2}=P_{3}/\pi_{3}=1/\pi_{3}$.

$P_{2}=1/2$ gives $\Pi/\pi_{1}=9/2$, i.e. $\pi_{1}=1/3$, and
$\pi_{2}=P_{2}/\pi_{1}=3/2$.  $P_{3}=1=\pi_{1}\pi_{2}\pi_{3}$ gives
$\pi_{3}=2$ and

$\pi_{5}= \Pi/(\pi_{1}\pi_{2}\pi_{3}\pi_{4})
       =\dfrac{3/2}{(1/3)(3/2)(2)(1/2)}=3$.

Low expression $\to$ high expression

$\pi_{1}=1/3,\;\pi_{2}=3/2,\;\pi_{3}=2,\;\pi_{4}=1/2,\;\pi_{5}=3$,

aFC ranks $1\equiv1/3$, $2\equiv1/2$, $3\equiv3/2$, $4\equiv2$, $5\equiv3$,

$1\;3\;4\;2\;5$,

$1/3-3/2-2-1/2-3$,

$E_{L}(2)=1/2,\;E_{R}(2)=9/2,\;T(2)=5$ and
$E_{L}(4)=1/2,\;E_{R}(4)=3/2,\;T(4)=2$.

The mirror $5\,2\,4\,3\,1$ is the same chromosome in opposite orientation.
The formal $h=5$ fit $1\,3\,4\,5\,2$ uses the fully mutant parental
haplotype $P_{5}=3/2$ for the WT individual, i.e. one copy has no crossover
between SNP1 and SNP5.  That is a terminal homozygous site and violates the
explicit requirement of one homologous crossover event on each copy between
the first and last SNP.  With the interior recombinant requirement
$2\le h\le4$ enforced the solution is unique up to reversal, $13425$. ∎

5.text:
With the WT diploid normalised to 2 let the cis effects in chromosomal
order be $\pi_{1}\dots\pi_{5}$ and $\Pi=\prod_{i}\pi_{i}=3/2$.
Put $P_{k}=\prod_{i\le k}\pi_{i}$.

Up to telomere reversal a gamete that carries a single switch with four
heterozygous loci and one homozygous mutant locus can be written as

$H_{L}:1\ldots h\;{\rm mut},\;h+1\ldots5\;{\rm WT}$,
$H_{R}:1\ldots h-1\;{\rm WT},\;h\ldots5\;{\rm mut}$,

$E_{L}=P_{h},\qquad E_{R}= \Pi/P_{h-1},\qquad
T(h)=E_{L}+E_{R}=P_{h}+\Pi/P_{h-1}=P_{h-1}\pi_{h}+\Pi/P_{h-1}$.

The statement is one homologous crossover event on each copy between
SNP1 and SNP5 and one homozygous mutant site with four heterozygotes.
That is exactly the recombinant pair above with a genuine switch on both
homologues, i.e. $1<h<5$, $h=2,3,4$.  A terminal $h=1$ or $h=5$ gives one
of the two gametes the parental full-mutant or full-WT haplotype and
hence zero crossovers on that copy.

Put $x=P_{h-1},\,a=\pi_{h}$.  $T(h)=2$ for the WT level F2 gives

$a x^{2}-2x+\Pi=0$,   $\Delta=4-4a\Pi\ge0\iff a\le2/3$.

Hence $a\in\{1/3,1/2\}$.  For an interior $h$ the admissible root is

$a=\pi_{h}=1/2,\qquad x=P_{h-1}=1$,

$P_{h}=1/2,\;Q_{h}=\Pi/x=3/2,\;T(h)=2$.

Up to reversal this is $h_{WT}=4$, $P_{3}=1$, $\pi_{4}=1/2$, $E_{L}=1/2$,
$E_{R}=3/2$.

Now $T(k)=5$ for the $2.5\times$ WT F2.  With $P_{3}=1$ the only interior
solution is $k=2$ :

$T(2)=P_{2}+\Pi/\pi_{1}=5$, $\;P_{2}=P_{3}/\pi_{3}=1/\pi_{3}$.

$T(2)=5$ with $P_{2}=1/2$ gives $\Pi/\pi_{1}=9/2$, so

$\pi_{1}=1/3$, $P_{2}=1/2\Rightarrow\pi_{2}=P_{2}/\pi_{1}=3/2$,

$P_{3}=1=\pi_{1}\pi_{2}\pi_{3}\Rightarrow\pi_{3}=2$,

$\pi_{5}= \Pi/(\pi_{1}\pi_{2}\pi_{3}\pi_{4})
       =\dfrac{3/2}{(1/3)(3/2)(2)(1/2)}=3$.

Hence low-expression $\to$ high-expression

$\pi_{1}=1/3,\;\pi_{2}=3/2,\;\pi_{3}=2,\;\pi_{4}=1/2,\;\pi_{5}=3$,

i.e. in aFC ranks $1\equiv1/3,\;2\equiv1/2,\;3\equiv3/2,\;4\equiv2,\;
5\equiv3$

$1\;3\;4\;2\;5$,

$E_{L}(2)=1/2,\;E_{R}(2)=9/2,\;T(2)=5$ and
$E_{L}(4)=1/2,\;E_{R}(4)=3/2,\;T(4)=2$.

The mirror $5\,2\,4\,3\,1$ is the same chromosome in the opposite
orientation.  The formal $h=5$ fit $1\,3\,4\,5\,2$ uses the parental
full-mutant haplotype $P_{5}=3/2$ for the WT-level individual, i.e. one
copy has no switch between SNP1 and SNP5, contradicting the explicit
requirement of one crossover on each copy.  With the stated interior
recombinant requirement the solution is unique up to reversal, $1\,3\,4\,2\,5$. ∎

1.text:
Diploid WT is normalised to 2 and on a haplotype
$E(M)=\prod_{i\in M}v_{i}$ with $\Pi=\prod_{1}^{5}v_{i}
=1/3\cdot1/2\cdot3/2\cdot2\cdot3=3/2$.

Up to telomere reversal a single crossover per homologue with four
heterozygous sites and one homozygous mutant site is

$H_{L}:1\ldots h\;{\rm mut},\,h+1\ldots5\;{\rm WT}$,
$H_{R}:1\ldots h-1\;{\rm WT},\,h\ldots5\;{\rm mut}$,

$E_{L}=P_{h},\qquad E_{R}= \Pi/P_{h-1}$,
$T(h)=E_{L}+E_{R}=P_{h}+\Pi/P_{h-1}=P_{h-1}v_{h}+\Pi/P_{h-1}$,
$P_{k}=\prod_{i\le k}v_{i}$.

A genuine crossover on *both* copies between SNP1 and SNP5 needs both
gametes to be recombinant, i.e. $1<h<5$, $h=2,3,4$, otherwise one of the
two homologues is the parental full-mutant or full-WT chromosome and has
no switch in the interval.

Put $x=P_{h-1},\,a=v_{h}$.  $T=2$ gives
$a x^{2}-2x+\Pi=0,\;\Delta=4-4a\Pi\ge0\iff a\le2/3$.
With the five cis values this is $a\in\{1/3,1/2\}$.  With $1<h<5$
the admissible interior solution is

$a=v_{h}=1/2,\qquad x=P_{h-1}=1$,

$P_{h}=a x=1/2,\;Q_{h}=\Pi/x=3/2,\;T(h)=2$.

Up to reversal this is $h_{WT}=4$,
$P_{3}=1,\;v_{4}=1/2,\;P_{4}=1/2,\;Q_{4}=3/2$,
$E_{L}=1/2,\;E_{R}=3/2$.

Now $T(k)=5$ for the $2.5\times$ WT F2. With $P_{3}=1$ the only interior
solution is $k=2$,

$T(2)=P_{2}+\Pi/v_{1}=5,\qquad P_{2}=P_{3}/v_{3}=1/v_{3}$.

$P_{2}=1/2$ gives $\Pi/v_{1}=9/2$, i.e.

$v_{1}=1/3,\qquad v_{2}=P_{2}/v_{1}=1/2/(1/3)=3/2$.

$P_{3}=1=v_{1}v_{2}v_{3}$ gives $v_{3}=2$ and

$v_{5}= \Pi/(v_{1}v_{2}v_{3}v_{4})
      =\dfrac{3/2}{(1/3)(3/2)(2)(1/2)}=3$.

Hence low-expression $\to$ high-expression left to right

$v_{1}=1/3,\;v_{2}=3/2,\;v_{3}=2,\;v_{4}=1/2,\;v_{5}=3$,

$E_{L}(2)=1/2,\;E_{R}(2)=9/2,\;T(2)=5$, $2.5\times$ WT,
$E_{L}(4)=1/2,\;E_{R}(4)=3/2,\;T(4)=2$, WT.

In aFC ranks $1\!\leftrightarrow\!1/3,\;2\!\leftrightarrow\!1/2,\;
3\!\leftrightarrow\!3/2,\;4\!\leftrightarrow\!2,\;5\!\leftrightarrow\!3$

$1\;3\;4\;2\;5$,

$1/3-3/2-2-1/2-3$, the mirror $5\,2\,4\,3\,1$ the same chromosome in
the opposite orientation. The terminal $h=5$ fit $1\,3\,4\,5\,2$ uses the
parental full-mutant haplotype $P_{5}=3/2$ for the WT individual, i.e.
one homologue has no switch between SNP1 and SNP5, contrary to one
crossover on each copy, and the $1\,4\,3\,2\,5$ ordering is arithmetically
impossible, $T(2)=2/3+9/2\neq5$. Up to reversal the unique interior
recombinant ordering is $13425$.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree 14325 is dead; the \(T(2)=31/6\) failure is decisive. The remaining issue is not whether 13425 is forced once we impose \(h\in\{2,3,4\}\), but whether the problem actually imposes that extra restriction.

For 13452, the two totals are exact:
- \(2.5\times\) WT: \(h=2\), prefix \(=\frac13\cdot\frac32=\frac12\), suffix \(=\frac32\cdot2\cdot3\cdot\frac12=\frac92\), total \(5\).
- WT level: \(h=5\), prefix \(=\frac13\cdot\frac32\cdot2\cdot3\cdot\frac12=\frac32\), suffix \(=\frac12\), total \(2\).

C5’s objection is not arithmetic; it is the additional interpretive claim that both sampled homologues must themselves show a visible recombinant switch. But the stated condition says the crossover is “between the first and last of the five SNPs.” A breakpoint between SNP4 and SNP5 is literally between SNP1 and SNP5. The wording does not explicitly say “strictly interior,” “not terminal,” or “both observed haplotypes must be non-parental.”

So unless C1/C5 can point to an explicit clause excluding the terminal breakpoint, 13452 remains an exact fit to both measured totals under the literal crossover interval. I would keep 13452.

3.text:
The diploid WT is normalised to 2 and with the cis aFCs in chromosomal
order $\pi_{1}\ldots\pi_{5}$

$\Pi=\prod_{i}\pi_{i}= \frac13\frac12\frac32 2 3 =\frac32$, 
$P_{k}=\prod_{i\le k}\pi_{i}$.

For a pair of recombinant homologues with a single switch per
homologue and four heterozygous sites and one homozygous mutant site we
can, up to telomere reversal, write

$H_{L}:1\ldots h\;{\rm mut},\,h+1\ldots5\;{\rm WT}$,
$H_{R}:1\ldots h-1\;{\rm WT},\,h\ldots5\;{\rm mut}$,

$E_{L}=P_{h}$, $E_{R}= \prod_{i\ge h}\pi_{i}= \Pi/P_{h-1}$,

$T(h)=E_{L}+E_{R}=P_{h}+\Pi/P_{h-1}=P_{h-1}\pi_{h}+\Pi/P_{h-1}$,
$E_{F2}=T(h)/2$.

A genuine single crossover on *each* copy between SNP1 and SNP5 needs
both gametes to be recombinant, i.e. $1<h<5$, $h=2,3,4$.  Put
$x=P_{h-1},\,a=\pi_{h}$.

$T=2$ for the WT level F2 gives

$a x^{2}-2x+\Pi=0$, $\qquad\Delta =4-4a\Pi\ge0\iff a\le2/3.$

Hence $a\in\{1/3,1/2\}$.  With an interior $h$ the admissible
solution is

$a=\pi_{h}=1/2$, $x=P_{h-1}=1$,

$P_{h}=1/2,\;Q_{h}=\Pi/x=3/2,\;T(h)=1/2+3/2=2$.

Up to reversal this is $h_{WT}=4$,

$P_{3}=1,\;\pi_{4}=1/2,\;P_{4}=1/2,\;Q_{4}=3/2$,

$E_{L}=1/2,\;E_{R}=3/2$.

Now $T(k)=5$ for the $2.5\times$ WT F2. With the interior requirement
$k=2$ is the only solution compatible with $P_{3}=1$.

$T(2)=P_{2}+\Pi/\pi_{1}=5$, $P_{2}= \pi_{1}\pi_{2}=P_{3}/\pi_{3}=1/\pi_{3}$.

The interior solution is $P_{2}=1/2$, $\Pi/\pi_{1}=9/2$,

$\pi_{1}=1/3$, $\pi_{2}=P_{2}/\pi_{1}=1/2/(1/3)=3/2$,

$P_{3}=1=\pi_{1}\pi_{2}\pi_{3}\Rightarrow\pi_{3}=2$,

$\pi_{5}=\Pi/(\pi_{1}\pi_{2}\pi_{3}\pi_{4})
      =\dfrac{3/2}{(1/3)(3/2)(2)(1/2)}=3$.

Low expression $\to$ high expression left to right

$\pi_{1}=1/3$, $\pi_{2}=3/2$, $\pi_{3}=2$, $\pi_{4}=1/2$, $\pi_{5}=3$,

$E_{L}(2)=1/2$, $E_{R}(2)=9/2$, $T(2)=5$ $2.5\times$ WT,
$E_{L}(4)=1/2$, $E_{R}(4)=3/2$, $T(4)=2$ WT.

In aFC ranks $1\leftrightarrow1/3$, $2\leftrightarrow1/2$,
$3\leftrightarrow3/2$, $4\leftrightarrow2$, $5\leftrightarrow3$,

$1\;3\;4\;2\;5$,

i.e. $1/3-3/2-2-1/2-3$, the mirror $5\,2\,4\,3\,1$ being the same
chromosome in opposite orientation.

The formal $h=5$ arithmetic fit $1\,3\,4\,5\,2$ uses for the WT
individual the haplotype pair $P_{5}=3/2$, $Q_{5}=1/2$.  $P_{5}$ is the
parental fully mutant haplotype and therefore has no crossover between
SNP1 and SNP5.  That is a terminal homozygous site $h=5$ and is
incompatible with one homologous crossover on each copy between the
first and last SNP, $2\le h\le4$.  The $1\,4\,3\,2\,5$ ordering is
arithmetically impossible, $T(2)=2/3+9/2\ne5$.  Up to telomere
reversal the unique interior recombinant ordering is $13425$, $52431$ in
the opposite orientation. ∎

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree that 14325 is not a serious contender. The real disagreement is still whether the terminal homozygous-mutant case is explicitly excluded. C1/C2/C3/C5 have shown that if we impose the extra condition \(2\le h\le4\)—i.e. the homozygous-mutant SNP must be strictly internal—then \(13425\) follows. I do not dispute that algebra.

But the problem statement says the crossover is “between the first and last of the five SNPs.” A breakpoint between SNP4 and SNP5 is still between SNP1 and SNP5. The statement does not explicitly say that both sampled F2 homologues must show a visible marker switch at the five SNPs, nor that the homozygous-mutant SNP must be non-terminal. Those are additional modeling assumptions.

For \(13452\), the arithmetic is exact under the endpoint reading:
- \(2.5\times\) WT: \(h=2\), prefix \(=\frac13\cdot\frac32=\frac12\), suffix \(=\frac32\cdot2\cdot3\cdot\frac12=\frac92\), total \(5\).
- WT level: \(h=5\), prefix \(=\frac13\cdot\frac32\cdot2\cdot3\cdot\frac12=\frac32\), suffix \(=\frac12\), total \(2\).

C5’s \(S(4)=9/2\) check does not refute this, because \(13452\) uses \(h=5\) for the WT-level individual, not \(h=4\). The only way to eliminate \(13452\) is to add the strict-internal condition. If the group is treating that condition as implicit, then \(13425\) is forced; if we stick to the literal interval wording, \(13452\) remains an exact fit. I would not drop \(13452\) without a clear textual exclusion of the terminal case.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m still not convinced \(13452\) should be excluded. The arithmetic for it is exact. The real disagreement is what “one homologous crossover event on each copy” means.

In meiosis, a single homologous crossover is between non-sister chromatids of the homolog pair; it does not force every gamete chromatid that emerges to be visibly recombinant at the scored SNPs. A gamete can carry a parental chromatid even though the meiosis itself had a crossover between SNP1 and SNP5. C5’s exclusion of the \(h=5\) branch requires reading “each copy” as “each inherited F2 chromatid is itself recombinant between the first and last SNP.” But the problem does not explicitly say that. It only says the crossover event is between the first and last SNP.

Under the meiosis-level reading, the WT-level individual in \(13452\) can use one recombinant copy with a breakpoint between SNP4 and SNP5, and one parental fully mutant copy, while the relevant meiosis still had a crossover in the SNP1–SNP5 interval. If we instead impose the stricter condition that both inherited chromatids must themselves be non-parental and visibly recombinant, then yes \(13425\) is forced. But that is an extra modeling assumption, not an explicit statement in the problem.

So unless C5/C1 can point to wording that literally requires both sampled chromatids to be recombinant at the scored SNPs, \(13452\) remains an exact-fit ordering and should not be discarded.

I’m still not convinced \(13452\) should be excluded. The arithmetic for it is exact. The real disagreement is what “one homologous crossover event on each copy” means.

In meiosis, a single homologous crossover is between non-sister chromatids of the homolog pair; it does not force every gamete chromatid that emerges to be visibly recombinant at the scored SNPs. A gamete can carry a parental chromatid even though the meiosis itself had a crossover between SNP1 and SNP5. C5’s exclusion of the \(h=5\) branch requires reading “each copy” as “each inherited F2 chromatid is itself recombinant between the first and last SNP.” But the problem does not explicitly say that. It only says the crossover event is between the first and last SNP.

Under the meiosis-level reading, the WT-level individual in \(13452\) can use one recombinant copy with a breakpoint between SNP4 and SNP5, and one parental fully mutant copy, while the relevant meiosis still had a crossover in the SNP1–SNP5 interval. If we instead impose the stricter condition that both inherited chromatids must themselves be non-parental and visibly recombinant, then yes \(13425\) is forced. But that is an extra modeling assumption, not an explicit statement in the problem.

So unless C5/C1 can point to wording that literally requires both sampled chromatids to be recombinant at the scored SNPs, \(13452\) remains an exact-fit ordering and should not be discarded.
